table.caption: Brisa Water Taxi, the only water taxi on a small lake: the most rides it can sell per hour at each price (invented data for practice)

imperfect-competition-s2.title: Four markets in one county
imperfect-competition-s2.text:
Read the descriptions of four invented markets.

  • Market W: thousands of farms grow the same variety of wheat, and any farm can sell all it wants at the market price.
  • Market X: one company holds the only license to pipe water to homes in the county, and no other firm may lay pipes.
  • Market Y: three bus lines carry nearly all riders between two cities; each watches the others before it sets its fares.
  • Market Z: forty hair salons compete, each with its own style, location and loyal customers, and a new salon can open in a few weeks.

items.q: Use the table. What is the marginal revenue of the third ride, in dollars?

why.correct: Marginal revenue is the change in total revenue divided by the change in quantity: $\text{MR} = \frac{24 - 18}{3 - 2} = 6$ dollars, which is less than the \$8 price of the third ride.

mistakes.why: \$8 is the price of the third ride. To sell it, Brisa also cuts the price of the first two rides by \$1 each, so the third ride adds only \$6 to revenue.
\$24 is the total revenue from three rides. Marginal revenue is the change in total revenue from the second to the third ride.

items.q: Use the table. Why is the marginal revenue of the third ride less than its \$8 price?
options: To sell it, Brisa must charge all riders \$8, giving up \$1 on each of the first two
The cost of the third ride is higher than the cost of the second ride
The demand for water taxi rides has decreased as the price fell
Each extra rider pays less than the rider before, but the earlier riders still pay the old \$9 price

why.correct: To sell a third ride Brisa lowers the price from \$9 to \$8 for every rider, so it gains \$8 from the new rider but loses \$1 on each of the two rides it could have sold at \$9: \$8 minus \$2 is \$6.
options: Right: the gain from the new ride is reduced by the price cut on the rides it already sold.
Cost does not enter marginal revenue; the table holds only revenue.
A lower price moves Brisa along its demand curve; demand itself has not changed.
With one price for everyone, the earlier riders also pay the new, lower price.

items.q: Use the table. What is the marginal revenue of the fifth ride, in dollars?

why.correct: $\text{MR} = \frac{30 - 28}{5 - 4} = 2$ dollars. Marginal revenue keeps falling, and it falls faster than the price.

mistakes.why: \$6 is the price of the fifth ride, not the revenue it adds. Subtract total revenue at four rides from total revenue at five.
\$30 is total revenue. Marginal revenue is the change in total revenue when one more ride is sold.

items.q: Use the table. Which statements are supported by the data? Select all that apply.
options: Brisa must lower its price to sell more rides, so it faces a downward-sloping demand curve.
After the first ride, marginal revenue is less than the price.
Marginal revenue equals the price for each ride, as for a price taker.
Total revenue falls each time Brisa lowers its price.

why.correct: Brisa faces a downward-sloping demand curve, so it is a price maker: marginal revenue (10, 8, 6, 4, 2) falls as rides rise and is below the price after the first ride.
options: Right: the price falls from \$10 to \$6 as rides rise from 1 to 5.
Right: for example, the second ride sells for \$9 but adds only \$8.
That holds only for a firm with a horizontal demand curve; Brisa's price falls as it sells more.
Total revenue rises from \$10 to \$30 in the table; marginal revenue is positive throughout.
Market W
Market Y
Market X
Market Z

why.correct: An oligopoly has a few large firms whose choices depend on one another: three bus lines that watch each other's fares.
options: Thousands of farms selling an identical product is perfect competition.
Right: a few firms, each watching the others before setting its fares.
A single seller with a legal barrier is a monopoly.
Many firms with differentiated products and easy entry is monopolistic competition.

items.q: In which market does a single firm have the most market power, and why?
options: Market Y, because its fares are higher than the other markets' prices
Market Z, because each salon has loyal customers
Market X, because it is the only seller and the license keeps rivals out
Market W, because the farms together sell far more output than any other market

why.correct: Market X has one seller and a legal barrier to entry, so buyers have no close substitute and no rival can enter: the firm can raise its price without losing every customer.
options: The size of a price says nothing about market power; three rivals limit each bus line.
Loyalty gives a salon a little market power, but forty rivals and easy entry limit it.
Right: one seller plus a barrier to entry gives the most market power.
Each farm is a price taker with no market power at all.

items.q: In which market does each firm face a horizontal demand curve?
options: Market X
Market Y
Market Z
Market W

why.correct: A wheat farm is a price taker: it sells all it wants at the market price, so its demand curve is horizontal at that price (d = MR = AR = P). The firms in the other three markets are price makers.
options: The only seller faces the whole downward-sloping market demand curve.
Each bus line can raise its fare and keep some riders, so its demand slopes down.
A salon with its own style can raise its price and keep some customers, so its demand slopes down.
Right: a price taker's demand is horizontal at the market price.

items.q: What gives each salon in Market Z some market power?
options: Product differentiation: no rival offers quite the same style and location
A high barrier to entry that keeps new salons from opening nearby
A county license that lets it, and no other salon, cut hair
Agreement with the other salons on what each one will charge for a cut

why.correct: Product differentiation: each salon's style and location make it a little different, so some customers stay when it raises its price. That is why its demand curve slopes down even with forty rivals.
options: Right: differentiation lets a salon raise its price without losing every customer.
The description says a new salon can open in a few weeks, so entry is easy.
That describes Market X, not the salons.
Nothing in the description says the salons coordinate their prices.

items.q: A firm has market power when it
options: sells more output than any other firm in the market
can raise its price without losing all of its customers
earns positive accounting profit
can sell as much as it likes at the market price set by others

why.correct: Market power is the ability to raise the price above marginal cost without losing all of its customers; such a firm is a price maker and faces a downward-sloping demand curve.
options: A large firm can still be a price taker if its product is identical to many rivals'.
Right: that is what makes it a price maker.
Accounting profit says nothing about whether the firm can set its own price.
That describes a price taker, which has no market power.

items.q: Which of the following is a barrier to entry?
options: Many buyers who are willing to pay a high price for the product
Low start-up costs, so a new firm needs little money to begin
A patent that makes one drug maker the sole seller of a medicine
A product that many firms can make with the same simple equipment

why.correct: A patent gives one firm the legal right to be the only seller of an invention for a period of years, so rivals cannot enter by copying it.
options: The number of buyers does not stop new sellers from entering.
Low start-up costs make entry easier, not harder.
Right: the law keeps other sellers out.
An identical product that anyone can make invites entry.

items.q: Keeling Glassworks is the only maker of a special glass for telescopes. If it wants to sell more glass each month, it must
options: raise the price it charges
keep its price where it is, since demand does not depend on price
match the price of rivals in its market
lower the price it charges

why.correct: A price maker faces a downward-sloping demand curve, so it sells more only by lowering its price: it chooses a price and quantity pair on its demand curve, not both freely.
options: A higher price moves it up its demand curve to a smaller quantity.
Buyers of the glass still buy less at a higher price.
It is the only maker; it has no rivals to match.
Right: on a downward-sloping demand curve, more is bought only at a lower price.

items.q: How does the marginal revenue curve of a firm with market power compare with that of a perfectly competitive firm?
options: It lies below demand, while a competitive firm's MR equals its price
It lies on the demand curve, as it does for a competitive firm
It lies above the demand curve, while a competitive firm's MR is below it
It is horizontal, while a competitive firm's MR slopes down

why.correct: For a price taker, d = MR = AR = P: every unit adds its price to revenue. A price maker must cut the price on all units to sell one more, so its marginal revenue curve lies below its downward-sloping demand curve.
options: Right: the price cut on earlier units pulls MR below the price.
That holds only for a price taker, whose price does not fall as it sells more.
MR can never exceed the price for a firm that must cut its price to sell more.
That has the two firms the wrong way round.

items.q: Label the axes and every curve on this graph of a firm with market power.

why.correct: Price and cost go on the vertical axis and quantity on the horizontal axis. The downward-sloping demand curve is D; the steeper line below it is MR; the U-shaped curves are MC and ATC, with MC crossing ATC at its minimum.

items.q: A firm with market power maximizes profit. Mark the point that shows the price it charges and the quantity it sells.

why.correct: Find the quantity where MR = MC, then go straight up to the demand curve: the price is read from demand, which lies above MR at that quantity.

items.q: Two new firms could make high-speed rail cars, but to reach a low average total cost a maker needs to produce for the whole national market. Why does this keep new firms out?
options: Diminishing marginal returns: each new firm adds less output
Economies of scale: a small entrant's ATC would be higher
The demand for rail cars is perfectly elastic
The firms already in the market earn zero economic profit

why.correct: Economies of scale: average total cost keeps falling as output grows, so one large firm can produce at a lower cost than a small entrant could. A newcomer would start with a higher ATC and could not match the price.
options: Diminishing returns describe one firm adding workers in the short run, not entry.
Right: falling long-run average total cost is a barrier to entry.
Perfectly elastic demand describes a price taker, not a market with one large producer.
Zero economic profit gives no reason to enter, but it is not a barrier that blocks entry.

items.q: A firm with market power earns positive economic profit year after year, while a perfectly competitive firm's economic profit returns to zero. What explains the difference?
options: The firm with market power has a lower marginal cost than rivals
Demand for its product keeps rising faster than costs over time
Barriers to entry keep rivals from competing the profit away
It produces where price equals marginal cost

why.correct: In perfect competition, profit draws in new firms until it is gone. Barriers to entry stop new firms from entering, so a firm with market power can keep its economic profit in the long run.
options: Lower costs could raise profit for a while, but without barriers, entry would still compete it away.
Rising demand is not a reason profit lasts; entry would follow it.
Right: entry is what drives a competitive firm's profit to zero.
A firm with market power produces where MR = MC, and its price is above MC.

items.q: Put the market structures in order from the most sellers to the fewest.
options: Perfect competition
Monopolistic competition
Oligopoly
Monopoly

why.correct: Perfect competition has very many sellers of an identical product; monopolistic competition many sellers of differentiated products; oligopoly a few large sellers; monopoly a single seller.

items.q: Build the answer: why does a firm with market power earn less from one more unit than the price of that unit?

why.correct: Because it faces a downward-sloping demand curve, it must cut its price on every unit to sell one more, so marginal revenue is less than the price.

specific.frame: It faces a ___ demand curve, so to sell one more unit it must lower the price on ___ units.
specific.model: Because the firm faces a downward-sloping demand curve, it must lower the price on all of its units to sell one more, so the extra unit adds less to total revenue than its price: marginal revenue is lower than price.

curve.label: Its demand curve
options: downward-sloping
horizontal

why.1: A horizontal demand curve belongs to a price taker, whose MR equals the price.

units.label: Which units
options: all of its
only the extra

why.1: With one price for every buyer, the earlier units are sold at the lower price too.

items.q: A mining company owns every known deposit of a rare mineral used in batteries. What is the source of its market power?
options: Product differentiation from heavy advertising of its brand
A large number of small rivals
A horizontal demand curve for its product
Control of a key resource that rivals cannot get

why.correct: Control of a key resource: no rival can produce the mineral without access to a deposit, so entry is blocked.
options: The mineral is the same whoever mines it; advertising is not what keeps rivals out.
Many rivals would reduce its market power.
A horizontal demand curve would mean no market power at all.
Right: owning every deposit keeps rivals out.
